942.name: Clear messaging in digital media
942.description: In this unit pupils will use a range of skills across several pieces of software. They will work between applications to create a poster and slides on a given theme. The unit is designed so that pupils can apply skills that they may have previously learnt as well as those learnt in the unit.
942.why: As pupils move from primary to secondary school, this unit supports their transition by building on digital skills developed in KS2. It helps them use the school network safely and respectfully while working across multiple applications. By creating a poster and presentation, pupils learn to combine text and images to communicate ideas clearly - skills they will apply across subjects throughout secondary school.
prior: Pupils should be familiar with how to perform online searches.
Pupils should have experience of using digital devices to create publications.
Pupils should have experience of combining text and images using digital devices to create artefacts that meet the needs of an audience.

944.name: Computer networks and data transmission
944.description: In this unit pupils will explore the impact networks have on our daily lives. They will define what a network is and explore the benefits of networking, before covering how data is transmitted across networks using protocols. They will investigate different types of network and hardware required.
944.why: As pupils begin secondary school, they are using the internet and connected devices more independently and in increasingly complex ways. At this stage, it is important that they understand what is happening behind the scenes when data is shared or services are accessed online. This unit builds a foundation for making informed decisions about privacy and security, helping pupils see how network design and data transmission affect their experience. Learning this now equips them to navigate technology critically and responsibly as its role in their lives expands.
prior: Pupils should have some experience of using websites.
Pupils should be able to describe the features of a network.
Pupils should be aware of how the internet facilitates online communication and collaboration.
Pupils should be able to describe the concept of privacy and how the internet does not always afford this.

945.name: Using media to gain support for a cause
945.description: During this unit, pupils develop their understanding of information technology and digital literacy skills. They will use the skills learnt across the unit to create a blog post about a real-world cause that they would like to gain support for.
945.why: As pupils become more independent in their use of technology, they need to understand how digital media shapes opinions and decisions. This unit helps them develop the skills to judge the reliability of online sources and understand copyright and licensing, preparing them to use content safely and ethically. By creating a blog to promote a cause, pupils practise communicating clearly and persuasively. These skills will be built on across subjects when presenting arguments, analysing sources and sharing ideas responsibly.
prior: Pupils recognise that content they use might be subject to copyright and its use restricted.
Pupils can identify the audience for content they create.
Pupils can combine text and images in a single document.
Pupils can adjust properties of text to make the content suitable for an audience.
Pupils can select images to enhance a written description and meet the needs of an audience.

946.name: Using fundamental programming constructs in a block-based language
946.description: In this unit pupils will build their confidence and knowledge of the key programming constructs (sequence, iteration, selection and variables). Learners will use Scratch to explore the key programming constructs firstly through editing pre-existing code and then by developing their own programs.
946.why: This unit reintroduces block-based programming to establish a shared foundation, allowing teachers to identify and address gaps in knowledge. It reinforces the key programming constructs: sequence, variables, selection, and count-controlled iteration. By securing these essentials now, pupils are better prepared for more complex programming in future units, including the transition from block-based to text-based languages later in KS3.
prior: Pupils should have experience of writing programs using block-based languages that use sequence, selection and iteration..
Pupils should be able to explain how algorithms describe the solution to problems.
Pupils should have experience of using events in programs as triggers to perform appropriate actions.

947.name: Physical computing using the micro:bit
947.description: In this unit, pupils will plan, develop, and evaluate a physical computing project. They will break down the project into smaller, easier-to-solve tasks. They will put these plans into action to create a working prototype that they use to evaluate their successes and identify future improvements.
947.why: Having already explored the core programming constructs of sequence, selection and iteration, pupils are now ready to apply these skills to real-world contexts through physical computing. This unit shows them that programming isn’t limited to on-screen outputs, helping them understand how code can control devices in the physical world. Pupils also develop their approach to project work by planning, implementing and reviewing solutions which are techniques that are valuable across subjects and essential for tackling more complex computing challenges in the future.
prior: Pupils will have created block-based programs that make use of subroutines.
Pupils will have programmed a physical computing device.
Pupils will have designed, implemented and reviewed a practical project.

948.name: Data modelling
948.description: By the end of this unit pupils should be able to model data within a spreadsheet. Pupils will progress from using basic formulas to using inbuilt functions. Pupils will apply sorting and searching techniques to data and explore how conditional formatting can be used to present data effectively.
948.why: Building on their understanding of variables from programming, pupils now apply this concept to organising and processing data in spreadsheets. This unit helps them see how raw data can be structured and transformed into meaningful information, allowing them to model real-life situations and draw conclusions. These skills are essential for future computing work and are widely used in subjects such as maths, science and geography, as well as in everyday tasks where data analysis supports decision-making.
prior: Pupils recognise that a spreadsheet stores numerical data
Pupils can enter data in to the cells of a spreadsheet
Pupils can identify different types of graphs and how to read them

949.name: Developing vector graphics
949.description: In this unit pupils will design graphics using vector graphic editing software. They will apply their skills by creating an illustration, a logo, and icons. Pupils will recognise that objects and be grouped and combined to create new elements and that vector drawings are made up of paths.
949.why: Having previously been introduced to vector graphics, pupils now deepen their understanding of how to create precise, scalable digital artwork. Building on earlier work with objects, layers and grouping, this unit develops pupils’ ability to design and refine complex graphics with accuracy and control. Learning these skills prepares pupils to consider how clear and professional visuals are essential for communicating ideas effectively across any context.
prior: Pupils recognise that digital devices can create and use image artefacts.
Pupils have experience of using drawing and painting packages to create both vector and bitmap images.
Pupils understand how the needs of an audience affect the way that information is best presented.

950.name: Computer systems and data science
950.description: In this unit pupils will explore the layers of computer systems from programs to the physical components that store and execute these programs. They will discover the fundamental binary building blocks that make up computer systems and how systems are evolving for developments such as AI.
950.why: As pupils’ use of technology becomes more advanced, it is important they understand how computer systems work and how different components interact. This unit takes pupils beyond simply using technology to exploring its underlying structure, from programs to operating systems. By comparing traditional computing systems with those that use artificial intelligence, pupils gain insights into the technologies shaping their world and develop the critical thinking needed to understand and question how these systems affect their daily lives and future learning.
prior: Pupils recognise that computer systems are formed from combinations of hardware components and software.
Pupils can identify common input and output devices used as part of computer systems.
Pupils understand that computers can be networked together to share resources.
Pupils understand that computer systems capture data and process it into useful output.

951.name: Developing for the Web
951.description: In this unit, pupils will explore the technologies that make up the internet and WWW. Starting with an exploration of the building blocks of the WWW, HTML, and CSS. They will construct a fully functioning website and discover how websites are catalogued for effective retrieval by search engines.
951.why: As pupils become more independent digital learners, it is important that they understand how the web works, not just how to use it. This unit introduces the building blocks of websites, HTML and CSS, helping pupils see how content is created and structured. By making their own website, they grow in confidence as digital creators while also learning how search engines organise and retrieve information. These skills strengthen problem-solving, creativity and digital literacy, supporting future learning across subjects.
prior: Pupils understand that web pages are rendered in web browsers.
Pupils recognise the features of effective website layout.
Pupils have created web pages using web page design software.
Pupils understand how search results are indexed by search engines.

953.name: Data representation: text and numbers
953.description: In this unit pupils will be introduced to binary digits and how they can be used to represent text and numbers. Pupils will perform conversions between binary and decimal numbers and how binary can be used to represent characters. They will explore how cryptography can be used to protect data.
953.why: At this stage, pupils are ready to move beyond simply using technology to understanding how it works at its core. Binary underpins everything a computer does, from processing text and numbers to storing data. By comparing it with the familiar decimal system, pupils can begin to see how computers represent information differently from humans. Learning about binary now gives pupils the insight to make sense of everyday technology, such as file sizes measured in kilobytes, megabytes and gigabytes, helping them become more informed and confident users of digital systems.
prior: Pupils recognise that data represents facts and objects.
Pupils can identify different formats of data.
Pupils recognise that instructions in computer systems are represented in binary.
Pupils can explain how simple logic circuits work.

954.name: Mobile app development
954.description: This unit takes pupils from designer to developer in order to create their own mobile app. Using App Lab from code.org, learners will familiarise themselves with the coding environment and have an opportunity to build on the programming concepts they used in previous units to undertake a project.
954.why: As pupils’ programming skills develop, they are ready to take on a more ambitious project that brings together the key constructs they have previously learned. This unit introduces a new block-based environment, giving pupils the chance to apply their knowledge of sequence, selection, iteration, and variables in a fresh context. By designing and building a mobile app, they experience the full process of planning, problem-solving and refining their work, showing them how programming can be used to create practical, real-world solutions.
prior: Pupils have experience of creating block-based programs that use sequence, selection and iteration.
Pupils have designed programs based the requirements of a project.
Pupils have created programs that allow data to be input, stored in a variable and then output once processed.

955.name: Introduction to Python programming
955.description: This unit introduces pupils to text-based programming with Python. Pupils start with programs involving input and output, and gradually move on to using arithmetic operations, randomness, selection, and iteration. Pupils will consolidate these skills in a project at the end of the unit.
955.why: Having built confidence with key programming constructs through block-based programming, pupils are now ready to apply these skills in a text-based language. This shift helps them understand how the same principles of sequence, selection, iteration, and variables are expressed in a different environment, developing their precision and problem-solving. Learning this now prepares pupils to take on more complex challenges, such as processing and analysing data stored in structures, which they will explore in later units.
prior: Pupils have some prior experience of programming, possibly in a block-based context.
Pupils should be aware that the sequence of commands can affect the outcome of the program.
Pupils are aware of the key programming constructs of sequence, selection, iteration and variables.
Pupils should be familiar with arithmetic operators.

956.name: Python programming with sequences of data
956.description: In this unit pupils will discover how data is represented and processed in sequences, such as lists and strings. They will cover a spectrum of operations on sequences of data, that range from accessing an individual element to manipulating the entire sequence though real world practical activites.
956.why: Having already written Python programs that handle input, output, calculations and control flow, pupils are now ready to explore how data can be stored and processed in sequences such as strings and lists. This unit develops their understanding of how to work with collections of data, moving from accessing individual elements to manipulating entire sets. Learning these techniques at this stage helps pupils see how structured data makes programs more efficient, preparing them to solve increasingly complex problems where handling and organising information is essential.
prior: Pupils can write text-based programs that use sequence, selection and iteration structures.
Pupils can create and use variables in text-based programs.
Pupils can input and output data in text-based programs.

957.name: 3D animation
957.description: In this unit pupils will discover how to create 3D animations using industry-standard software. They will gain a greater understanding of how 3D animation is used to make the media products that we consume. They will explore the basics of modelling, texturing, animating to create 3D models.
957.why: Having previously created and manipulated 2D vector images, pupils are now ready to explore how these skills translate into three dimensions. This unit introduces the fundamentals of 3D modelling and animation, showing how shapes, textures and movement combine to create realistic digital worlds. By working with tools used by professionals, pupils develop an understanding of how complex animations are built. Learning this now helps them appreciate the creative and technical processes behind modern media, preparing them to take on more ambitious digital projects with confidence and precision.
prior: Pupils understand what vector images are and have experience of creating them.
Pupils can find and use suitable digital artefacts.
Pupils can recognise the limitations placed on digital artefacts they find.

958.name: Using data science
958.description: In this unit pupils will discover how to use data to investigate problems and make changes to the world around them. Pupils will be exposed to both global and local data sets and gain an understanding of how visualising data can help with the process of identifying patterns and trends.
958.why: As pupils encounter more data in their daily lives, it is important they understand how it can be used to answer questions and drive meaningful change. This unit introduces the principles of data science, showing pupils how systematic approaches can reveal patterns and insights that might otherwise be missed. By exploring how data informs decisions within their school community, pupils see the value of evidence-based thinking and develop the critical skills needed to interpret information thoughtfully and responsibly.
prior: Pupils recognise the forms that data can take.
Pupils understand that data needs to be processed in to information to be useful.
Pupils recognise the differences between primary and secondary data.
Pupils understand how numerical data can be represented graphically.

959.name: Data representation: images and sound
959.description: In this unit, pupils will focus on digital media such as images and sounds, and discover the binary digits that lie beneath these types of media. They will explore how images and sound can be manipulated and consider the link between quality of images and sound and the resulting file size.
959.why: As pupils’ understanding of binary develops, they are ready to explore how it underpins the digital media they use every day. This unit helps them see that images and sound are not just files on a screen but are made up of binary digits that represent visual and audio data. By uncovering the hidden structure behind digital media, pupils gain a deeper appreciation of how technology works and why quality, size and format matter. This knowledge supports more informed and creative use of digital tools as they move on to complex media projects.
prior: Pupils recognise that computers use binary.
Pupils know that binary sequences are made from bits.
Pupils recognise that binary digits (bits) have two states, 1 and 0.
Pupils know that computers use binary to represent data and instructions.
Pupils can identify the impacts technology has on the way that people live their lives.

960.name: Introduction to cybersecurity
960.description: This unit takes pupils on a journey of discovery about techniques used by cybercriminals to steal data, disrupt systems and infiltrate networks. They will consider the value of data to organisations and what it is used for. They will look at social engineering techniques and common cybercrimes.
960.why: As pupils grow older and begin using a wider range of digital tools, they increasingly interact with networks that connect across the world. This unit develops their understanding of online threats, moving beyond the basic risks they have encountered so far. Pupils learn about the scale of these threats at individual, organisational and governmental levels and, crucially, the steps they can take to protect themselves and their data. This empowers them to act safely and responsibly, both in their personal lives and in future work settings where secure practices are essential.
prior: Pupils understand what networks are including the internet.
Pupils recognise ways they should stay safe online.
Pupils understand what computer systems are and why they need to communicate.

961.name: Machine learning using the micro:bit
961.description: This unit is designed to develop pupils programming skills in a new engaging context: physical computing, using the BBC micro:bit. They will get acquainted with the host of components built into the micro:bit, and write simple programs that use these components to interact with the physical world.
961.why: Applying programming skills to a physical computing context deepens pupils’ understanding of how code influences the world around them. This approach develops essential problem-solving, logical thinking and creative skills, helping pupils to see programming as more than just on-screen activity. By connecting their code to real, tangible outcomes, pupils gain a clearer sense of technology’s impact and begin to appreciate its role in shaping everyday life in an increasingly digital society.
prior: Pupils have experience of creating block-based programs.
Pupils understand how physical computers interact and control the environment they are used in.
Pupils can identify and use sequence, selection and iteration as part of programs.
Pupils can recognise and use variables and data structures in programs.
Pupils can explain what computer systems are.

970.name: Online safety
970.description: In this unit, pupils will evaluate the online world and their own internet activity for safety concerns in order to equip themselves with tools for protecting their online identities. They key takeaway of this unit is a repository of practical, risk-reducing steps that pupils can implement online.
970.why: As most pupils already have an online presence and experience of digital spaces, this unit encourages them to think more critically about their own behaviour and the actions of others online. It challenges pupils to engage with important debates, such as the balance between personal privacy and the powers of organisations or governments. By developing their own ideas and opinions, pupils grow into thoughtful and responsible digital citizens, able to navigate the online world with confidence and an understanding of their rights and responsibilities.
prior: Pupils can recognise how they should conduct themselves online.
Pupils can identify steps to take to ensure they use technology safely and responsibly.
Pupils understand that there are laws in place to deter people from misusing technology.

971.name: IT and the world of work
971.description: Pupils must be able to identify how the modern structure of the workplace will impact their future lives. This unit will facilitate a deeper comprehension of the methods employed by organisations and the impact the use of IT in the working environment has on all stakeholders.
971.why: As pupils prepare for life beyond school, they build on experiences of technology gained at home and in school to understand how IT shapes the modern workplace. This unit explores how digital tools support collaboration, remote work, and communication, and how these changes affect both organisations and employees. Pupils also consider issues of accessibility and inclusivity, helping them recognise the skills and awareness needed to thrive in a digital world of work.
prior: Pupils recognise how IT is used to support humans with tasks in the real world.
Pupils can use collaborative technology to share information.
Pupils can use spreadsheets to store and summarise data.
Pupils understand how to present information to meet the needs of an audience.

972.name: Using data science and AI tools effectively and safely
972.description: In this unit, pupils will explore how data science and AI tools are having an impact on our daily lives. They will develop an understanding of how to use these tools effectively as well as an awareness of the issues relating to trust, bias and misinformation.
972.why: AI, machine learning and data science are part of pupils’ daily lives through the apps, websites and tools they already use at home and in school. This unit helps them reflect on these experiences and understand how such technologies shape the world around them. Pupils learn to use these tools effectively while recognising potential risks, developing the judgment needed to become safe, discerning and responsible users of emerging digital systems.
prior: Pupils recognise that computer systems follow instructions to carry out tasks.
Pupils understand that AI is computer systems that are designed to perform tasks typically associated with human intelligence.
Pupils recognise that AI tools can be used to generate content.
Pupils have experience of modelling and processing data.

1477.name: Programming: sequence
1477.description: In this unit pupils will discover computers process instructions. They will recognise the function and tools IDEs provide for developing code and start to develop Python programa which follow a sequence. Pupils will create programs which deal with input and output and make variables to store values.
1477.why: As pupils begin their GCSE Computer Science course, it is vital they secure a strong understanding of the fundamental principles of programming. A clear grasp of how programs are structured and how data is managed equips pupils to tackle the increasingly complex challenges they will face. The unit concludes with a practical project, giving pupils the opportunity to bring these concepts together in a purposeful way which is an essential foundation for success in GCSE Computer Science and beyond.
prior: Pupils have experience of writing programs that use sequential instructions.
Pupils can identify different data types and recognise how they apply to programs that use variables.
Pupils understand how data and instructions are represented in computer systems.
Pupils have experience of debugging programs.

962.name: Algorithms
962.description: In this unit pupils will discover the computational thinking techniques; decomposition, abstraction and algorithmic thinking. They will reflect on differences between algorithms and computer programs and explore how algorithms can be represented. Pupils will explore the impact of algorithmic bias.
962.why: In this unit pupils develop the problem-solving and logical thinking skills that underpin success in computer science. Understanding algorithms helps them break down complex problems into manageable steps. By learning to represent algorithms through flowcharts, pseudocode and code, pupils gain the tools to think systematically and express solutions clearly. This deepens their understanding of how computers process instructions while also strengthening their reasoning and decision-making skills across subjects and everyday life.
prior: Pupils recognise computational thinking techniques.
Pupils have designed solutions to small-scale computing problems and implemented the solutions for use on a computer system.
Pupils have experience of writing text-based programs that use a combination of sequence, selection and iteration.

963.name: Programming: selection
963.description: In this unit pupils will explore the benefits of good programing practices and why subroutines are used in programs. They will create conditions in programs which use arithmetic, relational and logical expressions. They will develop their understanding of selection and explore nested selection.
963.why: Having already strengthened their understanding of sequences, pupils are now ready to explore how programs make decisions. Selection is introduced at this stage to help pupils move beyond linear code and begin writing programs that can adapt to different situations. Understanding how conditions control program flow and how logical expressions are evaluated develops their problem-solving and computational thinking. This ensures pupils can design more purposeful and responsive programs, laying the groundwork for tackling increasingly complex challenges in computer science.
prior: Pupils have created text-based programs that make use of sequence, selection and iteration.
Pupils can design and trace simple algorithms.
Pupils recognise that pseudocode and flowcharts are two ways that algorithms can be represented.
Pupils can use an IDE to assist in the development of programs.
Pupils recognise the component parts of selection statements including the use of conditions to control the flow of a program.

964.name: Computer Systems
964.description: In this unit pupils will discover the difference between general purpose and embedded systems. They will examine computer architecture and the components that make up a processor. Pupils will recognise the need for storage and be able to select a suitable storage device for a given purpose.
964.why: As pupils progress through the GCSE, it is important they understand what happens inside the computer systems they rely on every day. This unit gives them the knowledge to see beyond the screen, showing how simple logical operations form the foundation of all computing processes. By understanding how data is stored and managed, pupils can make informed decisions about storage solutions and appreciate the trade-offs between different technologies. Exploring the environmental impact of computing encourages pupils to think critically about how digital systems affect the world.
prior: Pupils recognise what computer systems are.
Pupils understand that computer systems read inputs and process them to produce outputs.
Pupils understand how computer system carry out instructions they are given.
Pupils can identify a variety of hardware that is used in computer systems.

965.name: Programming: iteration
965.description: In this unit pupils discover how iteration is used to replicate parts of a program. They will analyse the difference between count and condition controlled iteration and how trace tables can be used to trace through loops. They will explore data validation techniques and robust program design.
965.why: Pupils continue to revisit core programming concepts to strengthen and deepen their understanding. This unit focuses on iteration, building on familiar ideas while introducing greater complexity in how loops are applied to solve problems. By refining their skills in structuring and controlling the flow of programs, pupils create code that is more efficient to code and more adaptable. This progression prepares them to tackle more sophisticated, real-world programming tasks with confidence and independence.
prior: Pupils can write sequences in programs to solve a problem.
Pupils can write selection in programs to solve a problem.
Pupils understand how conditions are used to test the state of a program to use to control the flow of a program.
Pupils can create variables in a program with an appropriate data type.

1705.name: Boolean logic
1705.description: In this unit pupils will discover that Boolean logic is a way of describing circuits inside a computer. They will recognise logic gates as the building blocks of processors. They will be able to construct logic diagrams, truth tables and simplify Boolean expressions.
1705.why: Having already encountered logic gates when studying computer systems, pupils are now ready to deepen their understanding of how Boolean logic underpins the operation of modern processors. This unit helps them see how simple logical operations can be combined to solve problems, linking abstract logic to practical computing. Learning Boolean logic develops pupils’ ability to think critically, structure arguments, and apply systematic reasoning, which is valuable in everyday decision-making.
prior: Pupils recognise the Boolean operators AND, OR, NOT and the associated logic gate symbols.
Pupils can read a trace table for a logic gate.
Pupils will have used Boolean operators as part of conditions in text-based programming.
Pupils understand that a binary bit has two states, 1 and 0, and this can represent true and false.

1732.name: Programming: subroutines
1732.description: In this unit pupils will be introduced to structured programming. They will explore the differences between functions and procedures and use functions to return values in programs. They will be introduced to the concept of scope and how parameters can be used to reduce the need for global variables.
1732.why: Having already developed confidence with sequences, selection and iteration, pupils are now ready to structure their programs more effectively. This unit introduces subroutines, showing how breaking problems into smaller, reusable parts. Pupils build on their earlier use of built-in functions by learning to write their own, helping them appreciate the importance of decomposition in programming. Crucially, this way of thinking by dividing complex challenges into manageable steps and is a valuable skill beyond computer science, supporting problem-solving across subjects and in everyday life.
prior: Pupils can create programs that use sequence, selection and iteration.
Pupils have experience of designing algorithms for a given purpose.
Pupils have used subroutines as part of block-based programs.

966.name: Representation of numbers
966.description: In this unit pupils will be reminded of how the base-10 number system works before being introduced to the base-2 number system. They will perform conversions between binary and decimal and recognise the rules of binary addition and subtraction. They will be introduced to hexadecimal and its uses.
966.why: Understanding how data is represented and compressed helps pupils appreciate the invisible processes that make digital communication and storage possible. This unit strengthens logical thinking and numeracy while revealing how efficiency, accuracy and structure are central to all digital systems. Learning this now deepens pupils’ awareness of the design decisions that shape the technology they use every day.
prior: Pupils should recognise that data and instructions in a computer are represented in binary.
Pupils will be able to identify the place values of 8-bit binary numbers.
Pupils will be able to convert between binary and decimal values.

967.name: Programming: strings and lists
967.description: This unit introduces pupils to string-handling techniques, they will explore how a string can be iterated over using a loop and sliced to create substrings. Pupils will be introduced to arrays and lists and explore the differences between the two. They will manipulate with a variety of list methods.
967.why: As pupils become more confident programmers, they are ready to extend their understanding of how data can be organised and manipulated within programs. This unit builds on earlier work with text and data structures, introducing more sophisticated ways to store, access, and modify information. Understanding how to handle strings and lists enables pupils to create programs that are more efficient and adaptable. Developing these skills now strengthens their logical thinking and prepares them to design solutions that manage and process larger sets of data effectively.
prior: Pupils can create programs that use sequence, selection and iteration
Pupils recognise where data is stored in computer systems
Pupils understand the persistence of data stored on different storage devices

1738.name: Representation of text, images and sound
1738.description: In this unit, pupils will discover how letters, images and sounds are represented with binary digits. They will also explore the factors that impact the quality of those representations and investigate the effects these quality choices have on file size.
1738.why: As pupils’ understanding of how digital data is represented develops, they are ready to explore how computers store and manage different types of information. This unit helps pupils understand how text, images and sound are encoded, revealing how binary underpins digital media. By examining character sets and file compression, pupils begin to recognise the trade-offs between quality, file size and efficiency. Learning this now helps them appreciate the design choices that allow technology to balance performance, accessibility and user experience in the digital world.
prior: Pupils can describe why computers use binary digits to store data and instructions.
Pupils know that multiples of data can be abbreviated using number prefixes.
Pupils recognise that text, images and sound data are represented by sequencies of binary digits.
Pupils understand that text, images and sounds have properties that can be changed.

1750.name: Searching and sorting algorithms
1750.description: In this unit pupils will have opportunities to analyse, interpret, modify, and implement a range of searching and sorting algorithms. They will have the opportunity to compare the features and efficiency of these algorithms and make suggestions about the most suitable algorithm for a given task.
1750.why: As pupils’ understanding of algorithms develops, they are ready to explore how computers organise and process data efficiently. This unit introduces common searching and sorting algorithms, helping pupils see how these processes mirror everyday problem-solving. By analysing how algorithms differ in efficiency and suitability, pupils learn to think critically about the design and performance of computational solutions. Understanding these techniques at this stage strengthens logical reasoning and prepares pupils to make informed decisions when creating and optimising their own programs.
prior: Pupils can code algorithms that use sequence, selection and iteration.
Pupils can compare the features of algorithms that complete the same task.
Pupils understand how collections of data can be organised and stored in programs.

1480.name: Data compression
1480.description: In this unit pupils will be introduced to the concept of data compression and why it is needed. The will compare lossy and lossless compression methods and their typical uses. They will have the opportunity to compression methods such as run length encoding (RLE) and Huffman coding.
1480.why: At this stage, pupils are ready to think more critically about how digital information is managed in a world that depends on efficiency and communication. Understanding data compression helps them grasp the balance between quality, speed, and storage. Learning about how data is reduced and transmitted develops analytical thinking and decision-making, encouraging pupils to weigh trade-offs and justify choices. These skills extend beyond Computer Science, supporting logical reasoning and informed judgement across all areas of learning.
prior: Pupils recognise how data is stored in computer systems.
Pupils recognise that data is stored in a variety of forms.
Pupils recognise how common forms of data can be represented digitally.
Pupils understand how to summarise large quantities of bits using bytes and multiples.

969.name: Data science: AI and machine learning
969.description: This unit introduces pupils to the emerging field of data science. They will explore what AI systems are and the different categories of AI. The concept of machine learning and how models are driven by data will be explored. They will also consider the ethical and wider implications of AI systems.
969.why: Having previously explored the basics of artificial intelligence and machine learning, pupils now deepen their understanding of how these systems work and influence society. They examine predictive and generative AI, considering how such tools are trained and used. Reflecting on the social and ethical implications encourages pupils to think deeply about the role of AI in their lives and the responsibilities of those who design and use it.
prior: Pupils recognise that computer systems are the combination of hardware and software working together.
Pupils can describe how instructions in a computer system are executed.
Pupils can describe the relationship between planned algorithms and the programs that execute them.
Pupils are aware of the concept of analysing data to help solve a problem.

1478.name: Programming: sequence
1478.description: In this unit pupils will discover computers process instructions. They will recognise the function and tools IDEs provide for developing code and start to develop Python programa which follow a sequence. Pupils will create programs which deal with input and output and make variables to store values.
1478.why: As pupils begin their GCSE Computer Science course, it is vital they secure a strong understanding of the fundamental principles of programming. A clear grasp of how programs are structured and how data is managed equips pupils to tackle the increasingly complex challenges they will face. The unit concludes with a practical project, giving pupils the opportunity to bring these concepts together in a purposeful way which is an essential foundation for success in GCSE Computer Science and beyond.
prior: Pupils have experience of writing programs that use sequential instructions.
Pupils can identify different data types and recognise how they apply to programs that use variables.

1706.name: Boolean logic
1706.description: In this unit pupils will discover that Boolean logic is a way of describing circuits inside a computer. They will recognise logic gates as the building blocks of processors. They will be able to construct logic diagrams, truth tables and simplify Boolean expressions.
1706.why: Having already encountered logic gates when studying computer systems, pupils are now ready to deepen their understanding of how Boolean logic underpins the operation of modern processors. This unit helps them see how simple logical operations can be combined to solve problems, linking abstract logic to practical computing. Learning Boolean logic develops pupils’ ability to think critically, structure arguments, and apply systematic reasoning, which is valuable in everyday decision-making.
prior: Pupils recognise the Boolean operators AND, OR, NOT and the associated logic gate symbols.
Pupils can read a trace table for a logic gate.
Pupils will have used Boolean operators as part of conditions in text-based programming.

1733.name: Programming: subprograms
1733.description: In this unit pupils will be introduced to structured programming. They will explore the differences between functions and procedures and use functions to return values in programs. They will be introduced to the concept of scope and how parameters can be used to reduce the need for global variables.
1733.why: Having already developed confidence with sequences, selection and iteration, pupils are now ready to structure their programs more effectively. This unit introduces subroutines, showing how breaking problems into smaller, reusable parts. Pupils build on their earlier use of built-in functions by learning to write their own, helping them appreciate the importance of decomposition in programming. Crucially, this way of thinking by dividing complex challenges into manageable steps and is a valuable skill beyond computer science, supporting problem-solving across subjects and in everyday life.
prior: Pupils can create programs that use sequence, selection and iteration.
Pupils have experience of designing algorithms for a given purpose.

1739.name: Representation of text, images and sound
1739.description: In this unit, pupils will discover how letters, images and sounds are represented with binary digits. They will also explore the factors that impact the quality of those representations and investigate the effects these quality choices have on file size.
1739.why: As pupils’ understanding of how digital data is represented develops, they are ready to explore how computers store and manage different types of information. This unit helps pupils understand how text, images and sound are encoded, revealing how binary underpins digital media. By examining character sets and file compression, pupils begin to recognise the trade-offs between quality, file size and efficiency. Learning this now helps them appreciate the design choices that allow technology to balance performance, accessibility and user experience in the digital world.
prior: Pupils can describe why computers use binary digits to store data and instructions.

1749.name: Searching and sorting algorithms
1749.description: In this unit pupils will have opportunities to analyse, interpret, modify, and implement a range of searching and sorting algorithms. They will have the opportunity to compare the features and efficiency of these algorithms and make suggestions about the most suitable algorithm for a given task.
1749.why: As pupils’ understanding of algorithms develops, they are ready to explore how computers organise and process data efficiently. This unit introduces common searching and sorting algorithms, helping pupils see how these processes mirror everyday problem-solving. By analysing how algorithms differ in efficiency and suitability, pupils learn to think critically about the design and performance of computational solutions. Understanding these techniques at this stage strengthens logical reasoning and prepares pupils to make informed decisions when creating and optimising their own programs.
prior: Pupils can code algorithms that use sequence, selection and iteration.
Pupils can compare the features of algorithms that complete the same task.
Pupils understand how collections of data can be organised and stored in programs.

1479.name: Data compression
1479.description: In this unit pupils will be introduced to the concept of data compression and why it is needed. The will compare lossy and lossless compression methods and their typical uses. They will have the opportunity to compression methods such as run length encoding (RLE) and Huffman coding.
1479.why: At this stage, pupils are ready to think more critically about how digital information is managed in a world that depends on efficiency and communication. Understanding data compression helps them grasp the balance between quality, speed, and storage. Learning about how data is reduced and transmitted develops analytical thinking and decision-making, encouraging pupils to weigh trade-offs and justify choices. These skills extend beyond Computer Science, supporting logical reasoning and informed judgement across all areas of learning.
prior: Pupils recognise how data is stored in computer systems.
Pupils recognise that data is stored in a variety of forms.
Pupils recognise how common forms of data can be represented digitally.
Pupils understand how to summarise large quantities of bits using bytes and multiples.

976.name: Digital media
976.description: In this unit pupils will develop pre-production skills used in digital media. They will learn the importance of understanding client requirements, planning, developing timeframes and the steps involved in these processes. They will be exposed to a variety of software tools and learn how to use them.
976.why: This unit develops pupils' understanding of pre-production skills used in digital media industries. They will learn the importance of understanding the client's requirements, planning, developing timeframes and deadlines, and the techniques involved in these processes. They will then learn a number of the different software tools to fulfil basic client briefs. Pupils will apply this knowledge and develop their own digital media creation from a set of provided briefs. They will then assess each other's projects in terms of their effectiveness at meeting the aims of the brief.
prior: Pupils recognise the various forms that digital media can take
Pupils can evaluate the impact technology has on the lives of people
Pupils recognise how to stay safe online

977.name: Using physical computing to create a robot buggy
977.description: This unit introduces pupils to physical computing by building a robotic buggy. They will use a Raspberry Pi Pico microcontroller to explore inputs and outputs, and utilise a range of hardware components, including motors, reflective optical sensors, LEDs, and an ultrasonic sensor.
977.why: This unit progresses pupils' knowledge and understanding of physical computing. It starts with the creation of basic circuits and builds up their usage and confidence each lesson, as it incorporates programming a new piece of hardware with different inputs and outputs. By the end of the unit, pupils should have a good understanding of microcontrollers and embedded systems in general, as well as conceptual and practical experience of physically connecting input/output devices to GPIO pins, obtaining data from sensors, and using this data to make decisions.
prior: Pupils have experience of creating programs for a given purpose

978.name: Spreadsheets
978.description: In this unit pupils will explore how to use spreadsheets to store and manipulate data. They will use common functions and extract data to create visual representations using charts. Pupils will use spreadsheets to track and calculate income, make predictions, and answer “what if…?” questions.
978.why: Spreadsheets are a versatile tool used in a range of different contexts. As pupils reach the end of year 11 they will increasingly find more opportunities to use them in more complex ways. This unit will extend the basics of spreadsheets covered in previous units and provide pupils with the knowledge to build spreadsheets that will be robust and present data effectively. The culmination of the unit provides an opportunity for pupils to apply this understanding to a genuine scenario they may face when they leave school.
prior: Pupils can organise data in a spreadsheet
Pupils can create formulas to model data
Pupils can create graphs from data in a spreadsheet

979.name: Using IT in project management
979.description: Project management has numerous transferable skills for pupils, from simple time management to structured project management techniques. In this unit pupils will have the opportunity to develop invaluable skills in using common software tools and systems used for project management.
979.why: This unit draws together knowledge from a range of previous units throughout the whole curriculum and develops and understanding of how technology can be used to better organise and plan work. Using common office software, pupils leaving year 11 will appreciate how they can apply what they have learnt to real-life situations.
prior: Pupils can use spreadsheets to organise data
Pupils can recognise how IT is used in the world around us

1778.name: Programming: dictionaries and data files
1778.description: This unit introduces pupils to the new data structures of records and dictionaries. They will develop a Caesar cipher encryption program using a dictionary as a cipher wheel. Pupils will explore how data can be read from and written to files and how this data can be used within a program.
1778.why: As pupils enter the final stage of their GCSE programming journey, they are ready to manage data in more sophisticated and structured ways. This unit introduces new methods for storing and accessing information, encouraging pupils to think critically about how data is organised and used. Through applying structured approaches to records, lists and dictionaries, they strengthen their problem-solving and analytical thinking. Reflecting on how data is stored and retrieved helps pupils consider the growing role of data in modern computing and the responsibility of those who create and manage it.
prior: Pupils have experience of writing programs in a text-based language.

1483.name: Network fundamentals
1483.description: In this unit pupils will be develop their understanding of computer networks by looking at network models and the tasks performed by network hardware. They will discover the differences between wired and wireless transmission media and the factors that can affect the performance of a network.
1483.why: Having already explored the basics of networks, pupils are now ready to examine how they function in greater depth. Understanding network models, hardware and data transmission is essential for appreciating how modern communication systems operate. By analysing how networks are built and managed, pupils develop a deeper awareness of the systems that underpin digital communication and the importance of reliability, speed and security in an interconnected world.
prior: Pupils recognise that computers can be connected together in networks.

1795.name: Python programming project
1795.description: In this unit pupils will have the opportunity to apply the skills and knowledge they have developed in previous programming units by approaching a practical project. They will apply software design, product design and testing principles to take their project from initial design to working prototype.
1795.why: This unit brings together all of the programming concepts and techniques that pupils have developed throughout KS4. They will develop their project management skills to approach a practical programming project. They will learn software design principles as well as how to document development and testing throughout a programming project.

973.name: The internet and web technologies
973.description: In this unit pupils will explore how data travels across the internet. They will explore how protocols define communication between devices and the purpose of common network protocols. They will investigate the risks to networks and the methods that can be used to protect a network.
973.why: This unit further develops pupils' understanding of network communication by exploring how the internet is network of connected networks. They learn about the protocols that enable devices connected to the internet to communicate with one another and how these protocols are arranged in protocol stacks such as TCP/IP. Pupils will learn how a web browser works and the role of DNS and IP addressing in the WWW. The unit concludes by pupils exploring common threats to networks and the methods that can be used to protect networks.
prior: Pupils recognise how computers can be connected to form networks

1485.name: Databases and SQL
1485.description: This unit introduces pupils to databases and SQL, they will explore the key terms used in a database and why relational databases are used to eliminate the redundancy that can occur in a flat file database. They will explore SQL commands to retrieve, update, and delete data in a relational database.
1485.why: This unit introduces pupils to the world of databases and SQL. Pupils will have worked with datasets in KS3 but will not have experienced data management systems. Pupils will explore the key terms used in a database and learn why relational databases are used to eliminate the redundancy and inconsistencies that can occur in a flat file database. Pupils will explore increasingly challenging SQL commands where they retrieve, update, and delete data in a relational database. To conclude the unit pupils will investigate the legal, ethical and environmental impacts of data and data systems.

1486.name: Cyber threats and security
1486.description: This unit enables pupils to develop awareness of a range of cybersecurity threats that impact the world and us as individuals. They will explore different forms of attack, both non-automated and automated and how encryption tools can be used to protect communication.
1486.why: As pupils begin to rely more heavily on digital systems, it is vital that they understand the threats these systems face and how to defend against them. This unit builds awareness of cybersecurity, exploring both the human and technical factors behind attacks. By understanding the possible dangers and how organisations reduce vulnerabilities, pupils learn how to protect themselves and appreciate the importance of secure, resilient systems in today’s interconnected world.

975.name: HTML programming project
975.description: In this unit pupils will explore how websites are displayed within a browser using HTML and CSS. They will examine how websites are requested and delivered to our computer via the internet and the WWW. They will create the structure of a website using HTML and change the styling using CSS.

Pupils will gain an understanding of how websites are displayed within a browser using HTML and CSS, progressing on to using JavaScript to make these pages interactive. This unit is a culmination of pupils journey in learning programming by guiding them through a project that allows them to develop designing, writing, testing and refinement skills when developing a high-level text-based program.

5740.statement: Posters and signs should include lots of text information for the viewer to read.
5740.correction: Posters and signs should avoid too much detail when using text and images. This helps to clearly get a message across to the viewer at a glance and does not rely on them having to spend time looking at the detail.

5553.belief: Plans cannot change as a project progresses.
5553.statement: Plans cannot change as a project progresses.
5553.correction: Initial planning helps focus the purpose, content and layout of a product. However, due to feedback or changing needs, plans may need to be changed as a project progresses.

4251.correction: A logo is not a brand but a key part of a brand's or organisation's identity. A logo is a graphic that represents the visual identity of a brand or organisation.

3125.belief: The format and layout of slide decks must always be created from scratch each time you start a new document.
3125.statement: The format and layout of slide decks must always be created from scratch each time you start a new document.
3125.correction: Slide deck templates have pre-designed layouts and formatting that can be used as a starting point when creating new slide decks.

2005.belief: All content found on the World Wide Web is free to reuse.
2005.statement: All content found on the World Wide Web is free to reuse.
2005.correction: Content on the World Wide Web is subject to copyright and can be reused subject to licence agreements. Content found on the World Wide Web should be carefully chosen to ensure it is trustworthy and accurate.

2949.belief: Feedback is about telling people what has been done wrong and giving commands.
2949.statement: Feedback is about telling people what has been done wrong and giving commands.
2949.correction: Feedback should be supportive and constructive. Feedback should include details of what has gone well as well as suggestions to help improve the product.

4929.belief: On a network, servers, clients and routers have the same purpose.
4929.statement: On a network, servers, clients and routers have the same purpose.
4929.correction: Servers, clients and routers have distinct roles and functionalities in a network. They are not interchangeable and serve different purposes.

1900.belief: Computers only need protocols when sending emails or accessing websites.
1900.statement: Computers only need protocols when sending emails or accessing websites.
1900.correction: Protocols are essential for all sorts of activities, not just email or browsing websites. Protocols are also needed for streaming movies, playing online games, making video calls, etc. Anything being sent across a network needs to follow a protocol.

545.belief: Bandwidth is the speed of data being transmitted across a network. The higher the bandwidth, the faster data can be transferred between points in a network.
545.statement: Bandwidth is the speed of data being transmitted across a network. The higher the bandwidth, the faster data can be transferred between points in a network.
545.correction: Bandwidth is the maximum amount of data that can be transmitted at a time, not the time it takes to reach from one point to another. Higher bandwidth reduces the total transfer time of data but this is only noticable when there is a lot to transfer.

3832.belief: The internet is the same as the World Wide Web.
3832.statement: The internet is the same as the World Wide Web.
3832.correction: The World Wide Web is a service that is offered over the internet. The internet is the network that transfers data whilst the World Wide Web is the system of sharing information that people use.

2182.belief: Data packets from a complete message always follow the same route to their destination. They are then put back together in the order they are received.
2182.statement: Data packets from a complete message always follow the same route to their destination. They are then put back together in the order they are received.
2182.correction: Data packets are split and will be sent using the most efficient route at the time which often changes. Packets include data parts so they can be reassembled at the destination as long as the order of the packets is identified before being sent.

3833.belief: The internet of things (IoT) is only about smart homes and appliances.
3833.statement: The internet of things (IoT) is only about smart homes and appliances.
3833.correction: IoT are everyday devices that are connected to the internet and can communicate with each other. They might not collect data for the same purpose but they can collect information about how people use the devices.

691.belief: Blogs are just like any other website; they're all the same.
691.statement: Blogs are just like any other website; they're all the same.
691.correction: Blogs are more like online journals or news sites. Blogs are updated regularly, while websites might not change as often.

2995.belief: If I find an image online, I can use it however I want, as long as I don't say I created it.
2995.statement: If I find an image online, I can use it however I want, as long as I don't say I created it.
2995.correction: Just finding an image online doesn't automatically mean you can use it freely. Think of it like this: someone created that image, and they have rights to it, just like an author has rights to their book.

3787.belief: All information that is found on the internet is true.
3787.statement: All information that is found on the internet is true.
3787.correction: Anyone can create a website. Check who wrote it, when and if the facts are correct. Don't believe everything you see without checking first!

921.belief: If I change a few words from a website and use it as my own work it's not plagiarism.
921.statement: If I change a few words from a website and use it as my own work it's not plagiarism.
921.correction: Changing a few words isn't enough. Plagiarism is using someone's ideas without credit. Even if you rephrase, you must reference the original source.

10033.belief: Success criteria are only for the teacher to use when marking work. They don't help me.
10033.statement: Success criteria are only for the teacher to use when marking work. They don't help me.
10033.correction: They're not just for marking. Think of them like a checklist or a guide to help you create your best work. They tell you exactly what you need to do to succeed.

9028.belief: A rubric is just a checklist for the teacher. It doesn't help me write better blogs.
9028.statement: A rubric is just a checklist for the teacher. It doesn't help me write better blogs.
9028.correction: It's a guide to help you understand what makes a good blog post. It shows you the specific criteria, like clear writing or effective use of images, so you know what to focus on. Use it as a tool to improve your writing before submitting your work.

9572.belief: A sprite in Scratch can only have one sequence of code blocks.
9572.statement: A sprite in Scratch can only have one sequence of code blocks.
9572.correction: Sequences of code can be separated into subroutines and these subroutines can be called multiple times.

10778.belief: The value a variable holds cannot be updated and a computer remembers the previous values of variables.
10778.statement: The value a variable holds cannot be updated and a computer remembers the previous values of variables.
10778.correction: A variable can be updated during a program. Once the value of a variable is updated in a program, the previous value is overwritten.

5843.belief: A program can only follow one sequence of commands.
5843.statement: A program can only follow one sequence of commands.
5843.correction: Selection allows for a program to follow alternative paths depending on the criteria of the selection statement.

9183.belief: Selection statements can only check one condition at a time.
9183.statement: Selection statements can only check one condition at a time.
9183.correction: Complex conditions can be built into selection using a combination of comparison and logical operators. Logical operators join separate conditions and provide one complete statement that still evaluates to only True or False.

3884.belief: Iteration means a program will repeat something a set number of times.
3884.statement: Iteration means a program will repeat something a set number of times.
3884.correction: Count-controlled iteration will repeat a sequence of commands a set number of times. Condition-controlled iteration will repeat a sequence of commands until a condition is met and so the number of times it will repeat can never be predicted.

5851.belief: Programming constructs cannot be combined in the same code block.
5851.statement: Programming constructs cannot be combined in the same code block.
5851.correction: The programming constructs of sequence, selection and iteration can be combined within the same code block to make more complex programs.

1902.belief: Computers always have screens so that the user knows what processing has been performed.
1902.statement: Computers always have screens so that the user knows what processing has been performed.
1902.correction: Computers can carry actions using a variety of output devices. Physical computers are often used to carry out physical actions based on detected inputs so do not need a screen to display information.

4588.belief: The micro:bit can only show letters and numbers.
4588.statement: The micro:bit can only show letters and numbers.
4588.correction: The micro:bit's LED display can show more than letters and numbers. It can show shapes, images, and patterns. The display matrix can be programmed to output any desired pattern.

9188.belief: Sending and receiving radio signals broadcasts to all devices that have radio capability.
9188.statement: Sending and receiving radio signals broadcasts to all devices that have radio capability.
9188.correction: A radio channel can be set which means that only devices on that same channel will receive those broadcasts.

5545.belief: Planning a physical computing project slows you down and does not need to be thought of before starting what you want to make.
5545.statement: Planning a physical computing project slows you down and does not need to be thought of before starting what you want to make.
5545.correction: A plan helps you think through the steps, figure out what you need, and make sure your project turns out how you want it to. If you don't plan, you could end up making mistakes that will mean your project doesn't turn out how you would like.

771.belief: Building a physical computing project is just about putting the parts together. The code is not that important.
771.statement: Building a physical computing project is just about putting the parts together. The code is not that important.
771.correction: The code tells the hardware what to do and how to interact with the world, without the code it wouldn't move or do anything interesting!

5670.belief: There is no point in doing an evaluation once a project is finished as you are not going to go back and make any more changes.
5670.statement: There is no point in doing an evaluation once a project is finished as you are not going to go back and make any more changes.
5670.correction: Evaluations help learning by understanding your creative process and finding ways to improve. This often informs projects that you do in the future.

5231.belief: The order of column and row in a cell reference are unimportant as columns are labelled with letters and rows are labelled as numbers.
5231.statement: The order of column and row in a cell reference are unimportant as columns are labelled with letters and rows are labelled as numbers.
5231.correction: Spreadsheet cell references are presented as the combination of the column letter followed by the row number, (eg. A1, B2). If the order is interchanged any other part of the spreadsheet that references them will not be able to locate them.

6151.belief: Each time data is changed in a spreadsheet the formulas will also need to be changed.
6151.statement: Pupils may believe that each time data is changed in a spreadsheet the formulas will also need to be changed.
6151.correction: Using cell references within a formula means that the formula will recalculate when the values in those reference cells change.

2179.belief: Data and information are the same thing.
2179.statement: Data and information are the same thing.
2179.correction: Data and information are realted but are different. Data is raw facts and figures whilst information is data that has been processed to have meaning.

8752.belief: All range references in a spreadsheet needs to be the same as cell references in the format of column letter followed by row number (e.g. A1:A4).
8752.statement: All range references in a spreadsheet needs to be the same as cell references in the format of column letter followed by row number (e.g. A1:A4).
8752.correction: If you want to reference the whole column you can remove the row numbers (e.g. A:A). Note that this is the only case where cell references do not have to follow the column:row convention.

2978.belief: When a filter is applied to a data set the data that is filtered is removed permanently.
2978.statement: When a filter is applied to a data set the data that is filtered is removed permanently.
2978.correction: A filter can be applied to data to remove selected data from a data set. However, this data is not permanently removed, if the filter is taken off the data will still be there.

7727.belief: Conditional formatting can only be used to add background colour to a cell.
7727.statement: Pupils may think that conditional formatting can only be used to add background colour to a cell.
7727.correction: Conditional formatting can be used to apply a range of formatting a cell including the text of the cell itself.

10792.belief: Vector graphics are made from pixels and can lose quality when resized.
10792.statement: Vector graphics are made from pixels and can lose quality when resized.
10792.correction: Vector graphics are made from lines and shapes. They do not lose quality when resized.

3413.correction: Grouping objects can be reversed using ungroup. Combining objects is harder to reverse; only undo fixes combining.

938.belief: Changing a shape's path doesn’t change how it behaves — it’s still just a shape.
938.statement: Changing a shape's path doesn’t change how it behaves — it’s still just a shape.
938.correction: Editing a path changes the shape’s structure. Moving nodes changes the outline, allowing for new and more complex designs.

2465.belief: You don’t need a plan before starting a vector design — you can just make it up as you go.
2465.statement: You don’t need a plan before starting a vector design — you can just make it up as you go.
2465.correction: Planning helps you focus your design and choose the right tools and shapes before you start. Without a plan, it's easy to miss the goal or waste time making unnecessary changes.

10080.belief: SVG files are made of pictures, not code.
10080.statement: SVG files are made of pictures, not code.
10080.correction: SVG images are stored as text-based code. Each shape is written with instructions that describe its appearance, such as its size, colour and position on the canvas.

10793.belief: Vector images are better than bitmap images in every situation.
10793.statement: Vector images are better than bitmap images in every situation.
10793.correction: Vector and bitmap images are suited to different tasks. Vectors are best for simple, scalable designs like logos, while bitmaps are better for detailed images like photos.

1899.belief: All computers can do everything equally well.
1899.statement: All computers can do everything equally well.
1899.correction: General-purpose computers can run many programs, but single-purpose computers are designed to do one task very efficiently.

2089.belief: The CPU is the only important part of a computer.
2089.statement: The CPU is the only important part of a computer.
2089.correction: The CPU is an important part of a computer system but a computer also needs memory, input, output, and storage to work properly. All parts must work together as a system.

5217.belief: The operating system is just what you see on the screen.
5217.statement: The operating system is just what you see on the screen.
5217.correction: What you see on the screen is the graphical interface, but the operating system includes a lot more behind the scenes such as memory management, file systems, device control etc.

705.correction: Boolean logic is about truth values such as yes/no, true/false or (1/0).

2186.belief: Data science is just about collecting loads of data.
2186.statement: Data science is just about collecting loads of data.
2186.correction: Data science isn’t just about gathering data, it’s about understanding data and using it to make decisions or discoveries.

407.belief: Artificial intelligence and machine learning are the same thing.
407.statement: Artificial intelligence and machine learning are the same thing.
407.correction: Machine learning is a type of artifical intelligence that helps machines get better at tasks by learning from data, not just following pre-written instructions and rules.

1727.belief: Closing tags are optional and are just used to make the code easier to read.
1727.statement: Closing tags are optional and are just used to make the code easier to read.
1727.correction: Most tags need to be closed and require the use of a forward slash. This marks the beginning and the end of the content that the HTML tag should be applied to.

3624.belief: Images are stored inside HTML files as one document that is downloaded and displayed.
3624.statement: Images are stored inside HTML files as one document that is downloaded and displayed.
3624.correction: HTML only references image files, which are stored separately. When a web page is downloaded, the linked images are downloaded separately.

2129.belief: CSS rules must always include < > like HTML tags.
2129.statement: CSS rules must always include < > like HTML tags.
2129.correction: CSS uses just the tag name, without brackets.

9151.belief: Search engines search the whole internet live.
9151.statement: Search engines search the whole internet live.
9151.correction: Search engines use a pre-built index to deliver fast results.

11089.belief: The more words I add to a search, the better my results will be.
11089.statement: The more words I add to a search, the better my results will be.
11089.correction: Adding too many words can make a search too specific, limiting useful results. Use search operators like AND, OR, and NOT to refine the search and still find good information.

3569.belief: Hyperlinks only work on the homepage.
3569.statement: Hyperlinks only work on the homepage.
3569.correction: Hyperlinks are used across all pages, creating a fully navigable website. Any object on any HTML page can be made into a hyperlink.

2184.belief: Data is processed, organised and structured information that provides context and meaning.
2184.statement: Data is processed, organised and structured information that provides context and meaning.
2184.correction: Information is processed, organised and structured data that provides context and meaning. Data is facts and figures in their raw form.

8894.belief: The representation length does not include any spaces.
8894.statement: The representation length does not include any spaces.
8894.correction: The representation length is the total number of symbols in the sequence including spaces.

1901.belief: Computers process all types of information (text, images, video, etc.).
1901.statement: Computers process all types of information (text, images, video, etc.).
1901.correction: Ultimately, computers use sequences of symbols (0s and 1s) to represent all types of information.

663.belief: Binary uses the same place value system as decimal.
663.statement: Binary uses the same place value system as decimal.
663.correction: Binary is a base-2 number system, whereas decimal is a base-10 number system.

4544.correction: The order of prefixes from smallest to largest is kilo, mega, giga, tera.

5080.belief: Once encrypted, a message cannot be decrypted.
5080.statement: Once encrypted, a message cannot be decrypted.
5080.correction: A message can be encrypted and decrypted multiple times, this happens frequently during digital communications.

10677.belief: The user interface is only about how the app looks.
10677.statement: The user interface is only about how the app looks.
10677.correction: The user interface includes both how the app looks and how users interact with it. A good user interface is both visually clear and functionally simple.

2782.correction: Events only trigger code if an event listener is attached. Without one, the app will not respond.

10786.correction: Variables can store different types of data, including text (strings), numbers or Boolean values.

9136.belief: All screens run at the same time.
9136.statement: All screens run at the same time.
9136.correction: Only one screen is active at a time; users navigate between them when needed.

9595.belief: You should start creating an app without planning.
9595.statement: You should start creating an app without planning.
9595.correction: Planning first helps avoid confusion and mistakes and helps you build apps more efficiently.

5073.belief: Once the app runs it is finished.
5073.statement: Once the app runs it is finished.
5073.correction: Testing, debugging, and improving based on feedback are essential steps before finishing work on an app.

6998.statement: Pupils will modify their code to provide input directly in to the input() function, for example, user = input("Aisha"), rather than typing when asked as the program runs.
6998.correction: The computer follows the instructions of a program. Input that a user has to type in should only be entered when the program runs. This allows different users to provide different inputs without changing the program in any way.

7566.statement: Pupils often take user input for numerical values and then cannot perform arithmetic calculations on the data as the value is automatically stored as a string.
7566.correction: The int() function is used to convert a user's input to an integer so that calculations can then be performed. For example, age = int(input()) would allow a user to input their age in to a program.

10089.belief: The = symbol is used to check if a variable is equal to a value (comparison).
10089.statement: The = symbol is used to check if a variable is equal to a value (comparison).
10089.correction: The = symbol is used in Python for assignment. The == operator is used for comparison.

9601.belief: An if statement can only have two options.
9601.statement: An if statement can only have two options.
9601.correction: An if statement can be paired with elif and else statements to create multi-path selection. This allows for multiple paths to follow in a program.

10991.belief: A while loop is the most appropriate loop to use when you know exactly how many iterations will need to be performed.
10991.statement: A while loop is the most appropriate loop to use when you know exactly how many iterations will need to be performed.
